warmup.q: A processor reads the parameter waterEveryDays of data class Plant(val kind: String, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7). What can it learn about the default value?
options: That there is a default (hasDefault is true), but not what it is
Nothing: KSP can't tell a parameter with a default from one without
warmup.why: KSP shows declarations, and a default value is an expression, so it only tells you that one exists. TreeDemo in the first section prints waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault) and nothing more. The first and last options would need KSP to see inside the code, which it never does.

opening:
Picture the helper reading box labels before the move. "Desk lamp, one bulb, no shade" is easy. "Bookshelf, three shelves, a list of books" needs a word about what the list holds. Some labels use a shorthand that only makes sense once you look it up, and a few are written in another language.

In the last lesson, our processor read one thing from each label, the names of the constructor's properties, and wrote a card. A label holds much more: the type of each property, whether it may be missing (null), whether it has a default, and notes stuck on single lines. The easy trap is to print a type with toString(). It looks right on easy classes, and on the first tricky one it prints [typealias Litres].

In this lesson, we'll walk the whole tree of a class's label, print its typed shape correctly, read the values written on its sticky notes, and read a Java class too. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a helper reading labels: some easy, some in shorthand, one in another language. The tree gave us every declaration and no expression, resolve() turned each written type into the type it means, the notes gave their values by name, and the Java crate got a String! where Kotlin couldn't know more.

In your own code, find a place that prints or compares types as strings, a log line or a generated file, and check what it does with a ?, a type alias and a Java type.

Next, we'll stop writing generated code as strings. What happens to a string template when the type it prints lives in another package and needs an import?

sections.h: The label from top to bottom: a file, its classes and their members
sections.html:
A processor is the program that KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs during the build: it reads the classes that carry an annotation and writes new files. Everything KSP knows about your code comes as a tree of symbols, one node for each named thing. A declaration is a symbol you wrote yourself, such as a class or a function. Each file is the root of its own small tree. A KSFile holds KSClassDeclarations. Each class holds its properties (KSPropertyDeclaration), its functions (KSFunctionDeclaration) and any classes nested inside it, and each function holds its parameters (KSValueParameter). In the moving-house picture, the file is a box, and this tree is everything written on its label.

TreeDemo prints that tree for a small Kotlin file with Plant and Mirror, and for a Java file we'll meet in the last section:

file Rooms.kt  package=movemate
  class Plant  kind=CLASS  modifiers=[DATA]  origin=KOTLIN
    property kind: String
    property potLitres: Double
    property waterEveryDays: Int
    function component1(): String  origin=SYNTHETIC
    function component2(): Double  origin=SYNTHETIC
    function component3(): Int  origin=SYNTHETIC
    function copy(kind: String (hasDefault), potLitres: Double (hasDefault), waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault)): Plant  origin=SYNTHETIC
    function <init>(kind: String, potLitres: Double, waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault)): Plant  origin=KOTLIN
  class Mirror  kind=CLASS  modifiers=[]  origin=KOTLIN
    property widthCm: Int
    property heightCm: Int
    property glass: String
    function areaCm2(): Int  origin=KOTLIN
      property area: Int
    function <init>(widthCm: Int, heightCm: Int, glass: String): Mirror  origin=KOTLIN

Let's read it from the top. kind=CLASS comes from classKind, which tells a class from an INTERFACE, an OBJECT or an ENUM_CLASS; lesson 2's Check move used it. modifiers=[DATA] lists only the modifiers written in the source. Plant is public and final too, but nobody wrote those words, so they're not on the list. origin=KOTLIN says the symbol came from Kotlin source.

The functions hold two surprises. The constructor is a function named <init>; for a class with a primary constructor, primaryConstructor gives you the same node directly. And component1 to component3 and copy are listed too, marked origin=SYNTHETIC. Nobody wrote them, but a data class will have them, so KSP shows them.

Now look for what's missing. waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault) says the parameter has a default value, and nothing more: the 7 is an expression, and KSP shows no expressions. areaCm2(): Int is there with its name and return type, and inside it property area: Int, because a local val is a named declaration too. The multiplication widthCm * heightCm is nowhere. That's lesson 1's limit, now proved: the helper reads labels, never what's packed.

Java has had annotation processors since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. javac builds the same kind of tree for them, from Elements: a TypeElement for a class, an ExecutableElement for a method or constructor, and a VariableElement for a field or parameter. Walking a class's members looks much the same in both:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a class's members in a javac processor
for (Element member : cls.getEnclosedElements()) {
    switch (member.getKind()) {
        case FIELD -> messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.NOTE,
                "field " + member.getSimpleName() + ": " + member.asType());
        case CONSTRUCTOR, METHOD -> messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.NOTE,
                "method " + member.getSimpleName() + ((ExecutableElement) member).getParameters());
        default -> { }
    }
}
Kotlin
for (member in cls.declarations) {
    when (member) {
        is KSPropertyDeclaration -> logger.warn("property ${member.simpleName.asString()}: ${member.type}")
        is KSFunctionDeclaration -> logger.warn("function ${member.simpleName.asString()}" +
            member.parameters.map { it.name?.asString() })
        else -> {}
    }
}

One difference shows already. Java has no primary constructors and no data classes, so the Kotlin label says more than any javac processor could ever read from Java code.

KSP gives you every declaration and its type, and never an expression. Plan your processor around what the label says.

The tree prints types as text, such as Int and String. Printing them right is harder than it looks.

code.title: TreeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l03.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.ApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSFile import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSFunctionDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSPropertyDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSVisitorVoid import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream // Everything KSP shows a processor about one Kotlin file and one Java file: the label on each box, printed as a // tree. Look for what is there (names, types, hasDefault, a local val) and what is not (any expression). // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.TreeDemoKt /** A processor that prints the symbol tree of every source file once, in round 1. */ class TreeProcessor(private val lines: MutableList<String>) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var round = 0 override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (++round == 1) resolver.getNewFiles().forEach { it.accept(TreePrinter(), Unit) } return emptyList() } /** A visitor: KSP calls the visit function that matches each node; each one decides where to go next. */ inner class TreePrinter : KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures) { private var depth = 0 private fun line(text: String) { lines += " ".repeat(depth) + text } private fun children(nodes: Sequence<KSAnnotated>) { depth++ nodes.forEach { it.accept(this, Unit) } depth-- } override fun visitFile(file: KSFile, data: Unit) { line("file ${file.fileName} package=${file.packageName.asString()}") children(file.declarations) } override fun visitClassDeclaration(classDeclaration: KSClassDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("class ${classDeclaration.simpleName.asString()} kind=${classDeclaration.classKind} " + "modifiers=${classDeclaration.modifiers} origin=${classDeclaration.origin}") children(classDeclaration.declarations) } override fun visitFunctionDeclaration(function: KSFunctionDeclaration, data: Unit) { val parameters = function.parameters.joinToString(", ") { p -> "${p.name?.asString()}: ${p.type}" + if (p.hasDefault) " (hasDefault)" else "" } line("function ${function.simpleName.asString()}($parameters): ${function.returnType} origin=${function.origin}") children(function.declarations) // a function's own named declarations, such as a local val } override fun visitPropertyDeclaration(property: KSPropertyDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("property ${property.simpleName.asString()}: ${property.type}") } } } fun main() { val kotlin = SourceFile.kotlin( "Rooms.kt", """ package movemate data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) class Mirror(val widthCm: Int, val heightCm: Int, val glass: String) { fun areaCm2(): Int { val area = widthCm * heightCm return area } } """, ) val java = SourceFile.java( "MovingCrate.java", """ package movemate; public class MovingCrate { private final String label; public MovingCrate(String label) { this.label = label; } public String getLabel() { return label.trim(); } } """, ) val lines = mutableListOf<String>() val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(kotlin, java) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { TreeProcessor(lines) } } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") lines.forEach(::println) }

try.expect: The output in this section, then the Java file. areaCm2(): Int shows its name and return type, and property area: Int under it, because a local val is a declaration; the multiplication never appears. With the default, Mirror's constructor line shows glass: String (hasDefault), without the value. Without data, Plant's modifiers becomes [], and component1 to component3 and copy disappear, because only a data class gets them.

sections.h: Printing a type correctly: references, resolved types, nullability and arguments
sections.html:
Each parameter's type arrives as a KSTypeReference, the type as it's written in the source: String?, or Litres, not yet looked up. Calling resolve() turns it into a KSType, the type the compiler means, with its declaration (the class it names), its nullability and its type arguments. Resolving is a real lookup through imports, packages and type aliases. KSP's docs call it "one of the most expensive operations in the KSP API", so KSP resolves nothing until you ask.

In the picture, resolve() is the helper looking up a word on the label to see what it refers to: is Litres a box in this house, or shorthand for something else? Each lookup takes time. Here the picture breaks a little, too: unlike a person, KSP writes down every lookup a processor makes, because a later build needs to know which boxes each card depended on (lesson 7).

The label we want is the class's typed shape, Lamp(name: String, bulbs: Int, shade: String?). Two quick attempts come to mind: print the reference with toString(), or resolve it and print the declaration's name. ShapeDemo tries both, on a crate with tricky types and on a small Java class, next to the lab's typeText:

parameter                toString()                name only  typeText
Crate.shade              String?                   String     String?
Crate.books              List<String>              List       List<String>
Crate.water              [typealias Litres]        Litres     Litres
Crate.sizes              Map<String, List<Int?>>?  Map        Map<String, List<Int?>>?
Crate.odds               List<*>                   List       List<*>
Crate.onDrop             Function1<Int, Unit>      Function1  Function1<Int, Unit>
MovingCrate.label        (String..String?)         String     String!
MovingCrate.weightGrams  Int                       Int        Int

The name-only column fails at once. It drops every ? and every <...>, so shade becomes a String that can never be empty, which the first lamp without a shade will quickly disprove, and sizes loses its key and value types along with its ?. The toString() column looks right on easy types, and that's what makes it a trap. On the type alias, a second name for a type (typealias Litres = Double), it prints [typealias Litres]. On the Java class it prints (String..String?). KSP's toString() is a display form for people reading logs, not a promise about Kotlin syntax.

So we build the text ourselves from what KSType says, in three steps. First the name, type.declaration.simpleName. Then the type arguments, each printed the same way, because List<Int?> holds a type that needs exactly the same treatment: a recursive function. Then the nullability mark. Here is the core of it, with javac's closest equivalent first:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: printing a javac TypeMirror (javax.lang.model.type)
static String typeText(TypeMirror type) {
    if (type instanceof DeclaredType declared) {                  // a class type, maybe with arguments
        String name = declared.asElement().getSimpleName().toString();
        List<? extends TypeMirror> arguments = declared.getTypeArguments();
        if (arguments.isEmpty()) return name;
        return name + arguments.stream().map(Labels::typeText).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "<", ">"));
    }
    return type.toString();                                       // int, boolean and the other primitives
}
Kotlin
// the core of typeText; the lab adds the * and ! cases
fun typeText(ref: KSTypeReference): String {
    val type = ref.resolve()                                      // the expensive step
    val name = type.declaration.simpleName.asString()
    val arguments = if (type.arguments.isEmpty()) "" else
        type.arguments.joinToString(", ", "<", ">") { typeText(it.type!!) }   // the same, all the way down
    val mark = if (type.nullability == Nullability.NULLABLE) "?" else ""
    return name + arguments + mark
}

Two cases are left for the lab. A star projection, List<*> (a list of something unknown), has a type argument with no type at all: its type is null, so it.type!! would crash, and the argument's variance says STAR. And a platform type is a type from Java, where nothing says whether null is allowed; its nullability is PLATFORM, and Kotlin writes it String!. Printing Function1<Int, Unit> for (Int) -> Unit is fine for a label: both name the same type, and Kotlin simply has a shorter way to write it.

The Java twin can't print ? at all. A javac TypeMirror knows nothing about nullability, because Java's type system has none; Java code marks it with annotations such as @Nullable instead. That's one of the Kotlin facts a KSP processor keeps and a Java processor never sees.

Resolve each reference once, then build the text from the resolved type: name, arguments, mark. toString() is for your eyes, not for your output.

Each line of the label now prints right. Some boxes also carry notes with values written on them.

code.html: package workbench.ksp.l03.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.ApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.getConstructors import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l03.typeText // Three ways to print a parameter's type, side by side, for every constructor parameter of the @Label classes: // toString() what the type reference prints by itself // name only the resolved type's declaration name, the first thing people try // typeText lesson 3's typeText (the reference one, or yours with -Pmine=l03) // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.ShapeDemoKt class ShapeTable(private val rows: MutableList<List<String>>) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { for (cls in resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Label").filterIsInstance<KSClassDeclaration>()) { val constructor = cls.primaryConstructor ?: cls.getConstructors().first() for (p in constructor.parameters) { val written = p.type.toString() val nameOnly = p.type.resolve().declaration.simpleName.asString() val ours = try { typeText(p.type) } catch (e: NotImplementedError) { "(not done yet)" } rows += listOf("${cls.simpleName.asString()}.${p.name!!.asString()}", written, nameOnly, ours) } } return emptyList() } } fun main() { val kotlin = SourceFile.kotlin( "Crate.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Label typealias Litres = Double @Label class Crate( val shade: String?, val books: List<String>, val water: Litres, val sizes: Map<String, List<Int?>>?, val odds: List<*>, val onDrop: (Int) -> Unit, ) """, ) val java = SourceFile.java( "MovingCrate.java", """ package movemate; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Label; @Label public class MovingCrate { public MovingCrate(String label, int weightGrams) { } } """, ) val rows = mutableListOf(listOf("parameter", "toString()", "name only", "typeText")) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(kotlin, java) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { ShapeTable(rows) } } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") val widths = (0..3).map { column -> rows.maxOf { it[column].length } + 2 } rows.forEach { row -> println(row.mapIndexed { i, cell -> cell.padEnd(widths[i]) }.joinToString("").trimEnd()) } }

sections.h: Reading the values on a sticky note: annotation arguments and their defaults
sections.html:
An annotation, a note written with @ on a declaration, can carry values, called its arguments: @Room("study") says which room a box goes to. MoveMate's lesson 3 note, @Handling, has three, each of a different kind and each with a default:

Java
public enum Care { NORMAL, GENTLE, UPRIGHT }

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)
public @interface Handling {
    Care care() default Care.NORMAL;
    boolean stackable() default true;
    Class<?> packWith() default Object.class;
}
Kotlin
enum class Care { NORMAL, GENTLE, UPRIGHT }

@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.SOURCE)
annotation class Handling(
    val care: Care = Care.NORMAL,
    val stackable: Boolean = true,
    val packWith: KClass<*> = Any::class,
)

The two declarations line up closely. Java writes each argument as a method with a default; Kotlin writes it as a constructor property with a default value. One difference: Java's "no particular class" is usually Object.class, and Kotlin's here is Any::class.

KSP gives each annotation on a symbol as a KSAnnotation, and its arguments as a list of KSValueArgument, each with a name and a value. What kind of object the value is depends on the argument's type. A String or a Boolean arrives as itself. A class argument (KClass) arrives as a KSType. An enum value arrives as a KSClassDeclaration, the declaration of the enum entry, so its simpleName is UPRIGHT.

Running it showed two details worth remembering. The list holds every parameter of the annotation, including the ones the source didn't write, filled in with their defaults; such an argument has origin=SYNTHETIC, which isDefault() checks. And the list isn't in declaration order. KSP lists the written arguments first, in the order they were written, and the defaults after them. So look arguments up by name, never by position:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: reading annotation values in a javac processor
Map<? extends ExecutableElement, ? extends AnnotationValue> written = handling.getElementValues();
Map<? extends ExecutableElement, ? extends AnnotationValue> all =
        processingEnv.getElementUtils().getElementValuesWithDefaults(handling);
for (var entry : all.entrySet()) {
    String name = entry.getKey().getSimpleName().toString();       // care, stackable, packWith
    Object value = entry.getValue().getValue();   // an enum: a VariableElement; a class: a TypeMirror
    boolean isDefault = !written.containsKey(entry.getKey());
}
Kotlin
val handling = annotationNamed(cls, "workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Handling") ?: return null
fun argument(name: String) = handling.arguments.first { it.name?.asString() == name }   // by name

val care = argument("care").value as KSClassDeclaration       // an enum value: the entry's declaration
val stackable = argument("stackable").value as Boolean        // a Boolean: itself
val packWith = argument("packWith").value as KSType           // a class: a KSType
val chosen = !argument("stackable").isDefault()               // false when the source didn't write it

javac draws the same line differently: getElementValues() holds only what was written, and getElementValuesWithDefaults fills in the rest, so a default is whatever the first map lacks.

Finding the annotation itself needs one more bit of care. Its shortName is the name as written, Room, and another package could have a Room of its own. The lab's given annotationNamed compares the short name first, which costs nothing, and resolves annotationType to its full name only when the short name matches: the cheap check first, then the expensive one, as KSP's docs advise.

LabelDemo runs the whole lesson 3 processor on a lamp and on a bookshelf marked @Room("study") @Handling(care = Care.UPRIGHT, packWith = Lamp::class). Here is the bookshelf's label:

--- movemate/BookshelfLabel.kt
// Generated by LabelProcessor from Bookshelf. Do not edit.
package movemate

object BookshelfLabel {
    const val SHAPE: String = "Bookshelf(shelves: Int, books: List<String>)"
    const val ROOM: String = "study"
    const val HANDLING: String = "care=UPRIGHT, stackable=true (default), packWith=Lamp"
}

stackable wasn't written, so it says true (default). The lamp's label has a SHAPE line and nothing else, because the lamp carries neither note.

Look annotation arguments up by name, and ask isDefault() before you assume the user chose a value.

So far every label was written in Kotlin. MoveMate also has one box from a Java team.

code.html: package workbench.ksp.l03.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l03.LabelProcessorProvider // The whole @Label processor on two MoveMate classes, in memory: what KSP said, the label files it wrote, and // one label read back through the result's class loader. Reference processor by default; -Pmine=l03 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.LabelDemoKt fun main() { val moveMate = SourceFile.kotlin( "MoveMate.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Label import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room import workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Care import workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Handling @Label data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Label @Room("study") @Handling(care = Care.UPRIGHT, packWith = Lamp::class) class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) """, ) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(moveMate) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += LabelProcessorProvider() } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") result.messages.lines().filter { "[ksp]" in it }.forEach(::println) val generated = compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin") generated.walk().filter { it.isFile }.sorted().forEach { file -> println("--- ${file.relativeTo(generated).invariantSeparatorsPath}") print(file.readText()) } if (result.exitCode == KotlinCompilation.ExitCode.OK) { val handling = result.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.BookshelfLabel").getField("HANDLING").get(null) println("--- BookshelfLabel.HANDLING is: $handling") } }

try.expect: First the labels in this section, ending with --- BookshelfLabel.HANDLING is: care=UPRIGHT, stackable=true (default), packWith=Lamp. With stackable = false only, the line reads care=NORMAL (default), stackable=false, packWith=Any (default): the two unwritten arguments come back with their defaults, marked. Without @Room, the label keeps SHAPE and HANDLING and loses ROOM.

sections.h: A Java box, and a visitor that walks any box
sections.html:
KSP reads Java source files in the same module too, through the same API. Their symbols say origin=JAVA. Here is the rest of TreeDemo's output, for a small Java class:

file MovingCrate.java  package=movemate
  class MovingCrate  kind=CLASS  modifiers=[PUBLIC]  origin=JAVA
    property label: (String..String?)
    function getLabel(): (String..String?)  origin=JAVA
    function <init>(label: (String..String?)): MovingCrate  origin=JAVA

Three things differ from a Kotlin class, and the label meets two of them. Java has no primary constructor, so primaryConstructor is null, and the label falls back to the first constructor that getConstructors() finds. Java fields come back as properties, even the private label. And a Java String is a platform type, (String..String?): Kotlin can't tell whether it may be null, so the label prints String!. A Java int, which can never be null, comes back as a plain Int.

In the picture, this is a box labeled in another language. The same helper can read it, but a few words are fuzzy, and the helper says so with a ! instead of guessing.

The real build needs no extra setup for it. The lesson 3 playground keeps MovingCrate.java next to the Kotlin classes, and ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin writes MovingCrateLabel.kt for it: a Kotlin file describing a Java class, which Java code then reads as MovingCrateLabel.SHAPE.

Now the visitor that TreeDemo used. A visitor is an object with one function per kind of node: visitFile, visitClassDeclaration, visitFunctionDeclaration and so on. Calling node.accept(visitor, data) makes KSP call the function that matches the node's kind, so the visitor never needs a chain of is checks. Both compilers offer the same pattern:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac element visitor (javax.lang.model.util, JDK 16+)
class TreePrinter extends SimpleElementVisitor14<Void, Void> {
    @Override
    public Void visitType(TypeElement type, Void unused) {
        line("class " + type.getSimpleName());
        type.getEnclosedElements().forEach(child -> child.accept(this, null));  // go to the children yourself
        return null;
    }

    @Override
    public Void visitVariable(VariableElement field, Void unused) {
        line("field " + field.getSimpleName() + ": " + field.asType());
        return null;
    }
}
// start the walk: element.accept(new TreePrinter(), null)
Kotlin
inner class TreePrinter : KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures) {
    override fun visitClassDeclaration(classDeclaration: KSClassDeclaration, data: Unit) {
        line("class ${classDeclaration.simpleName.asString()}")
        classDeclaration.declarations.forEach { it.accept(this, Unit) }   // go to the children yourself
    }

    override fun visitPropertyDeclaration(property: KSPropertyDeclaration, data: Unit) {
        line("property ${property.simpleName.asString()}: ${property.type}")
    }
}
// start the walk: file.accept(TreePrinter(), Unit)

KSVisitorVoid does nothing by default. Each of its functions has an empty body, so the visitor goes only where your code sends it, by calling accept on the children. javac's SimpleElementVisitor14 behaves the same way; its sibling ElementScanner14 is the one that visits every child for you.

Write it as KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures), passing the processor's apiFeatures. The official quickstart still writes KSVisitorVoid(), and that spelling has been deprecated since KSP 2.3.12. On 2.3.14 it compiles with the warning 'constructor(): KSVisitorVoid' is deprecated. The same goes for validate() without arguments, which lesson 5 meets.

A visitor earns its keep when one walk must handle many kinds of node, as TreeDemo does. The lab's labels only ever look at a class and its constructor, so plain functions read better there.

A visitor sends each node to the function for its kind. Use one when the walk is the job, and plain functions when you know where you're going.

That's the whole label read: the tree, the types, the notes, and the boxes from Java.

try.title: Read a Java class in the real build
steps: Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateKt, then the Java twin with -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateJava.

In labs/ksp/app/src/l03/java/workbench/ksp/app/l03/MovingCrate.java, change both int weightGrams to Integer weightGrams (the field and the constructor parameter) and getWeightGrams() to return Integer. Predict the new shape, run the KSP task again, then undo the change.

code.title: MoveMate.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l03 import workbench.ksp.annotations.Fragile import workbench.ksp.annotations.Label import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room import workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Care import workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Handling // Lesson 3, the real build: the @Label processor reads these labels, and the Java class next door, // labs/ksp/app/src/l03/java/workbench/ksp/app/l03/MovingCrate.java. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin -Pmine=l03 run KSP alone with yours; it works even on the stub // then open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l03/ // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateKt -Pmine=l03 once your lab passes @Label data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Label @Room("study") @Handling(care = Care.UPRIGHT, stackable = false, packWith = Lamp::class) class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) @Label @Room("conservatory") @Handling(care = Care.GENTLE) data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) @Label @Room("hall") class Mirror(val widthCm: Int, val heightCm: Int, @Fragile val glass: String) { // the processor sees this function's name and return type, never the arithmetic inside it fun areaCm2(): Int = widthCm * heightCm } fun main() { println(LampLabel.SHAPE) println("${BookshelfLabel.SHAPE} -> ${BookshelfLabel.ROOM}, ${BookshelfLabel.HANDLING}") println("${PlantLabel.SHAPE} -> ${PlantLabel.ROOM}, ${PlantLabel.HANDLING}") println("${MirrorLabel.SHAPE} -> ${MirrorLabel.ROOM}") println(MovingCrateLabel.SHAPE) }

alt.title: MoveMateJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l03; // The Java twin: Java reading the labels that KSP generated in Kotlin. A `const val` in an object compiles to a // public static final field, so Java reads LampLabel.SHAPE directly. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateJava -Pmine=l03 public class MoveMateJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(LampLabel.SHAPE); System.out.println(BookshelfLabel.SHAPE + " -> " + BookshelfLabel.ROOM + ", " + BookshelfLabel.HANDLING); System.out.println(PlantLabel.SHAPE + " -> " + PlantLabel.ROOM + ", " + PlantLabel.HANDLING); System.out.println(MirrorLabel.SHAPE + " -> " + MirrorLabel.ROOM); System.out.println(MovingCrateLabel.SHAPE); } }

try.expect: The file holds const val SHAPE: String = "MovingCrate(label: String!, weightGrams: Int)". Both demos print five labels, from Lamp(name: String, bulbs: Int, shade: String?) to MovingCrate(label: String!, weightGrams: Int), and the Java twin reads them as plain static fields such as LampLabel.SHAPE. With Integer, the shape becomes MovingCrate(label: String!, weightGrams: Int!): a boxed Integer may be null, so it's a platform type too.

compare.title: Reading a parameter's type and an annotation's values: javac and KSP

java.title: LabelProcessor.java
java.html: // Closest Java equivalent: javac's model (javax.lang.model) ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(cls.getEnclosedElements()).get(0); for (VariableElement parameter : constructor.getParameters()) { TypeMirror type = parameter.asType(); // already resolved, no nullability at all line(parameter.getSimpleName() + ": " + typeText(type)); } for (AnnotationMirror note : cls.getAnnotationMirrors()) { var all = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getElementValuesWithDefaults(note); for (var entry : all.entrySet()) { Object value = entry.getValue().getValue(); // enum: VariableElement, class: TypeMirror line(entry.getKey().getSimpleName() + "=" + value); } }

kotlin.title: LabelProcessor.kt
kotlin.html: val constructor = cls.primaryConstructor ?: cls.getConstructors().first() for (parameter in constructor.parameters) { val type = parameter.type.resolve() // resolved on request, with its nullability line("${parameter.name!!.asString()}: ${typeText(parameter.type)}") } for (note in cls.annotations) { for (argument in note.arguments) { // defaults included, after the written ones val value = argument.value // enum: KSClassDeclaration, class: KSType line("${argument.name?.asString()}=$value" + if (argument.isDefault()) " (default)" else "") } }

compare.note: The two models match almost one to one: TypeElement to KSClassDeclaration, ExecutableElement to KSFunctionDeclaration, VariableElement to KSValueParameter or KSPropertyDeclaration, AnnotationMirror to KSAnnotation. Three differences are real. A javac TypeMirror arrives already resolved, while KSP hands you a reference and resolves it only when you call resolve(), because resolving is expensive. A TypeMirror has no nullability, because Java has none, while a KSType says NULLABLE, NOT_NULL or, for Java types, PLATFORM. And the value kinds differ: javac gives an enum constant as a VariableElement, KSP 2 gives the enum entry's KSClassDeclaration; both give a class as a type (TypeMirror, KSType). Kotlin's version also gets the primary constructor directly; Java has to pick one.

worked.title: Print Map<String, List<Int?>>? by hand, the way typeText does

steps.say: Start at the outside. Resolve the reference once and read the three facts the label needs: the declaration's name, the type arguments, and the nullability.
steps.code: // 1. the outer type val type = ref.resolve() type.declaration.simpleName.asString() // "Map" type.arguments // [String, List<Int?>], both INVARIANT type.nullability // NULLABLE

alt.html: // 1. the outer type (javac: already resolved) DeclaredType type = (DeclaredType) parameter.asType(); type.asElement().getSimpleName(); // Map type.getTypeArguments(); // [java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>] // no nullability: Java's types don't carry any

steps.say: The first argument is simple: String, no arguments, NOT_NULL, so it prints String. The second is a List with one argument, Int, whose nullability is NULLABLE, so the inner call prints Int? and the list prints List<Int?>. Each argument goes through the same function, which is why it's recursive.
steps.code: // 2. each argument, with the same function typeText(stringRef) // "String" typeText(listRef) // "List" + "<" + typeText(intRef) + ">" = "List<Int?>"

alt.html: // 2. each argument, with the same function typeText(stringMirror) // "String" typeText(listMirror) // "List" + "<" + typeText(integerMirror) + ">" = "List<Integer>"

steps.say: Put the outer parts back together: the name, the arguments joined with , inside < and >, and the mark for the outer nullability. The result is Map<String, List<Int?>>?, the type exactly as written. The Java twin prints Map<String, List<Integer>>, with no marks, because javac never had them to give.
steps.code: // 3. assemble "Map" + "<String, List<Int?>>" + "?" // "Map<String, List<Int?>>?"

alt.html: // 3. assemble "Map" + "<String, List<Integer>>" // "Map<String, List<Integer>>"

steps.say: Count the resolutions: four, one per reference, for Map, String, List and Int. Each is a lookup, and KSP records each one, because an incremental build, one that redoes only what changed, must know which files this label read (lesson 7). That's the reason for the rule: resolve each reference once, and only the ones you need.

lab.title: The @Label processor: read the typed shape and the notes
steps: Read LabelProcessor.kt. Moves 1 (Find), 2 (Check) and 4 (Write) are given, written the way you wrote them in lesson 2, and so are labelSource and annotationNamed. Your part is move 3, Read: the four functions at the end of the file.

Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin -Pmine=l03. It prints w: [ksp] l03 not done yet: 3. Read: the class name and each constructor parameter ... and the build passes (add --rerun if the task says UP-TO-DATE and prints nothing).

1. Read, the type: write typeText. Resolve the reference, then print the declaration's simple name, the type arguments in <...> by calling typeText again on each (a * for Variance.STAR, whose type is null), and the mark: ? for NULLABLE, ! for PLATFORM, nothing for NOT_NULL.

1. Read, the shape: write shapeOf. Use primaryConstructor, or getConstructors().firstOrNull() for a Java class. Print each parameter as name: type, add = ... when hasDefault, and start it with @Fragile when annotationNamed(parameter, "workbench.ksp.annotations.Fragile") finds the note.
1. Read, the notes: write roomOf (the name argument of @Room) and handlingOf (care, stackable and packWith, in that order, each followed by (default) when isDefault() is true).

1. Prove: run the tests until all five pass. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin -Pmine=l03, open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l03/MovingCrateLabel.kt, and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateKt -Pmine=l03.
From memory: close the file and write typeText again on paper, all four cases. Then compare it with yours.
hints: ref.resolve() gives a KSType: declaration.simpleName.asString() is the name, arguments the type arguments, nullability the mark.
A KSTypeArgument has a variance and a type, which is a KSTypeReference?. Call typeText(arg.type!!) for every variance except Variance.STAR, and put out or in in front for COVARIANT and CONTRAVARIANT.
An enum argument's value is a KSClassDeclaration, so (value as KSClassDeclaration).simpleName.asString() gives UPRIGHT. A class argument's value is a KSType; read its declaration.simpleName.
isDefault() is an extension function: import com.google.devtools.ksp.isDefault. getConstructors() is one too: import com.google.devtools.ksp.getConstructors.
Look arguments up by name, annotation.arguments.first { it.name?.asString() == "care" }, because the written ones come before the defaults.

drill.title: Print a type from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write typeText(ref: KSTypeReference): String from memory: the name, the type arguments (recursively, with * for a star), and ?, ! or nothing for the nullability. Then write the javac version for a TypeMirror, and say in one sentence why it has no ?. Compare with the answer.

answer.html: fun typeText(ref: KSTypeReference): String { val type = ref.resolve() val arguments = if (type.arguments.isEmpty()) "" else type.arguments.joinToString(", ", "<", ">") { arg -> when (arg.variance) { Variance.STAR -> "*" Variance.COVARIANT -> "out " + typeText(arg.type!!) Variance.CONTRAVARIANT -> "in " + typeText(arg.type!!) Variance.INVARIANT -> typeText(arg.type!!) } } val mark = when (type.nullability) { Nullability.NULLABLE -> "?" Nullability.PLATFORM -> "!" Nullability.NOT_NULL -> "" } return type.declaration.simpleName.asString() + arguments + mark }

alt.title: Labels.java
alt.html: // no ?: Java's type system has no nullability, so a TypeMirror can't carry it static String typeText(TypeMirror type) { if (type instanceof DeclaredType declared) { String name = declared.asElement().getSimpleName().toString(); List<? extends TypeMirror> arguments = declared.getTypeArguments(); if (arguments.isEmpty()) return name; return name + arguments.stream().map(Labels::typeText).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "<", ">")); } if (type instanceof WildcardType) return "?"; // Java's star return type.toString(); // primitives }

recap: KSP shows a tree of declarations: KSFile, KSClassDeclaration (with classKind, the modifiers written in the source, and primaryConstructor), KSPropertyDeclaration, KSFunctionDeclaration and KSValueParameter. A data class's copy and componentN appear as SYNTHETIC.
A KSTypeReference is the type as written; resolve() gives the KSType it means, with its declaration, arguments and nullability. Resolving is expensive, so resolve each reference once.
Build a type's text yourself: the name, each argument the same way (a star has no type), then ?, nothing, or ! for a Java platform type. toString() prints [typealias Litres] and (String..String?).

Annotation arguments arrive as themselves (String, Boolean), as a KSType (a class) or as the entry's KSClassDeclaration (an enum value). Defaults are in the list with isDefault() true, after the written ones, so look them up by name.
Java sources in the module are read too (origin=JAVA): no primary constructor, private fields as properties, and platform types.
The limit: KSP never shows an expression. hasDefault says a default exists, never its value, and a function's body is closed to it.

explain.prompt: A teammate's processor builds its labels with parameter.type.toString(), and the tests pass. Explain why that's still a bug waiting to happen, and what typeText does instead.
explain.answer: toString() on a type reference is KSP's display form for people reading logs. It happens to look like Kotlin for simple types, so tests with String and List<String> pass, but it isn't a promise. On a type alias it prints [typealias Litres], and on a Java type it prints (String..String?), neither of which is how anyone writes the type. typeText resolves the reference once to get the KSType it means, then builds the text from its parts: the declaration's simple name, the type arguments printed by the same function (with * for a star, which has no type), and the nullability mark, ? for nullable, ! for a Java platform type, nothing for not-null. That way the output depends only on facts the API guarantees, and each reference is resolved just once, which matters because resolving is expensive.

deeper.html:
A few more facts about the label, for the day you need them.

getDeclaredProperties() lists only the class's own properties, while getAllProperties() includes inherited ones too, and needs type resolution to find them, so it costs more. The same split exists for functions. Both getDeclared... helpers are extension functions in com.google.devtools.ksp that filter declarations.

You can often avoid resolving at all. A reference's element is the type as written, and for a class name, (ref.element as? KSClassifierReference)?.referencedName() gives the written name without a lookup. KSP's docs suggest filtering that way first, and resolving only the references you still care about, because every resolution is both slow and recorded as a dependency for incremental builds.

Nested classes need care. simpleName of Kitchen.Drawer is just Drawer, and splitting qualifiedName at dots can't tell a package from an outer class. For a label, drop the package from the qualified name; for generated code, lesson 4's KotlinPoet does it properly.

Comparing types has a trap for Java hands. KSP's a.isAssignableFrom(b) asks whether a b can be stored in an a, so Any.isAssignableFrom(String) is true. javac's Types.isAssignable(t1, t2) asks whether a t1 can be stored in a t2, so the arguments come in the opposite order. And == on KSType includes nullability: String? is not equal to String.

Finally, getAnnotationsByType(Room::class) looks convenient, because it hands you a real annotation instance. But it's marked experimental, and reading a class argument through it throws KSTypeNotPresentException, because the class it names may not be compiled yet. Read KSAnnotation.arguments, as this lesson does.
